questions.question: The energy price cap limits…
options: The unit rates and standing charges on default tariffs
questions.explanation: It caps rates, not your total bill. Use more and you pay more.

questions.question: An energy standing charge is…
options: A fixed daily charge, however much you use
questions.explanation: You pay it even if you use no energy.

questions.question: Who sets the energy price cap?
questions.explanation: Ofgem reviews the cap regularly.

questions.question: When a broadband or mobile contract ends, prices often…
options: Rise unless you renegotiate or switch
questions.explanation: Providers must tell you when your contract ends, so use that to haggle.

questions.question: A SIM-only deal makes the most sense when…
options: You own your phone and don't need a new one
You want a free new phone
questions.explanation: Keeping your phone and going SIM-only is often far cheaper.

questions.question: The council tax discount for a single adult living alone is…
questions.explanation: Adults living alone usually get 25% off.

questions.question: Option 1: a phone contract at £45/month for 24 months. Option 2: buy the phone for £600 plus SIM-only at £12/month. How much does option 2 save over 24 months?
Broadband “social tariffs” are for…
options: People on certain benefits, such as Universal Credit
questions.explanation: They're cheaper packages for eligible households.

questions.question: A water meter often saves money when…
options: Fewer people live in the home than there are bedrooms
questions.explanation: Smaller households often pay less on a meter.

questions.question: Paying for energy by monthly Direct Debit is usually…
options: Cheaper than paying when the bill arrives
questions.explanation: Suppliers usually charge less for Direct Debit.

questions.question: Council tax is based on:
options: The valuation band of your home
questions.explanation: Every home is assigned a band based on its value; the band sets the amount.

questions.question: People living alone can usually get a council tax discount of:
questions.explanation: Single-adult households typically get 25% off their council tax.

questions.question: Full-time students living only with other full-time students are usually:
questions.explanation: Households of only full-time students are generally exempt; apply to the council rather than assuming.

questions.question: Your energy bill is unusually high. First checks:
options: Compare the meter reading to the bill and check it wasn't an estimated reading
Turn everything off for a month
questions.explanation: Estimated readings cause bill shocks; submitting actual readings gets the bill recalculated.

questions.question: Why do suppliers ask for regular meter readings?
options: So bills reflect real usage instead of estimates that build up debt or credit
questions.explanation: Actual readings keep your account accurate, avoiding a nasty catch-up bill later.

questions.question: A smart meter's main benefit is:
options: Automatic readings, so accurate bills and real-time usage visibility
questions.explanation: Smart meters send readings automatically; they show usage but don't change your tariff by themselves.

questions.question: Moving home with a fixed energy deal usually means:
options: The deal usually ends, so check exit fees and the new home's tariff before moving
questions.explanation: Fixed deals are attached to the property, so plan ahead: check exit fees and new-home options.

questions.question: Since 2019, switching energy supplier typically takes:
questions.explanation: The energy switching process was standardised to around 5 working days, including a 14-day cooling-off period.

questions.question: What is the energy price cap?
options: A maximum you can ever pay
A limit on the unit price and standing charge suppliers can charge on standard tariffs
questions.explanation: The cap limits unit rates, not your bill; use more, pay more. It changes periodically.

questions.question: Your total energy bill depends on:
options: Unit price, standing charge and how much energy you use
questions.explanation: Two homes on identical tariffs can have very different bills because usage differs.

questions.question: Direct debits for energy are typically reviewed and adjusted to:
options: Match your expected annual usage, so they can rise after a review or in winter
questions.explanation: Suppliers smooth your annual usage across 12 payments and rebalance when usage or prices change.

questions.question: In shared rented housing, an energy account in your name means:
options: Housemates' debt is never your problem legally
You're liable for the bills, so get written agreements and meter readings when people move in or out
questions.explanation: The named account holder is liable, so sort arrangements in writing at move-in and move-out.

questions.question: The one-click switching rules for broadband mean:
options: Your new provider handles the switch and tells your old one
You must call your old provider repeatedly to cancel
questions.explanation: UK one-click switching means the new provider manages the switchover, including notifying the old one.

questions.question: Mid-contract price rises for broadband and mobile are often linked to:
options: Inflation (CPI or RPI) plus a fixed percentage, as written in your contract
questions.explanation: Many contracts allow CPI plus an extra percent each year; check your contract's small print before signing.

questions.question: You're out of contract on broadband. You should expect to:
options: Be moved to a cheaper rate
Pay noticeably more than new-customer deals, so it pays to renegotiate or switch
questions.explanation: Out-of-contract rates are often much higher; switching or asking for a better deal is worth the few minutes.

questions.question: Switching energy supplier while owing them money:
options: Can be possible; small debts may transfer to the new supplier, while larger debts can block the switch
questions.explanation: Debts under a threshold can move with you; bigger arrears usually must be settled first.

questions.question: The Priority Services Register is for:
options: People who need extra support, like those with medical equipment or disability, giving extra help from suppliers
questions.explanation: It gives free extra support such as advance notice of outages and accessible information.

questions.question: Which usually works out cheaper for water, if your usage is low?
options: Rateable value billing is always cheaper
A water meter, if you use relatively little water
questions.explanation: Households with low usage or fewer occupants than bedrooms often save with a meter; many suppliers let you trial one.

questions.question: A TV Licence is legally needed in the UK to:
options: Watch or record live TV, and to use BBC iPlayer
Have a TV aerial in the loft
questions.explanation: Streaming on-demand services other than iPlayer doesn't need one; live TV and iPlayer do.

questions.question: Cancelling a direct debit for a service you still use leads to:
options: The company chasing payment and possible late fees or service loss, so cancel the service properly
questions.explanation: Cancel the subscription or contract first, then the direct debit; doing only the latter doesn't end the debt.

questions.question: Auto-renewal on insurance policies often results in:
options: A higher premium than new customers get, so compare before silently renewing
questions.explanation: Loyalty often costs more in insurance; new-customer prices undercut renewals, so shop around each year.

questions.question: When you switch energy supplier, your supply:
options: Gets cut off for a week
Continues seamlessly through the same pipes and wires; only the billing company changes
questions.explanation: Switching is a billing change only; the physical supply never stops.

questions.question: Annual or irregular bills like car tax or insurance are easier to afford if you:
options: Set aside a monthly amount so the bill never lands as a shock
Put them on a credit card and forget
questions.explanation: A sinking fund for annual bills turns a lumpy cost into a smooth monthly amount.

questions.question: If you can't pay an energy bill, the right first step is:
options: Contact the supplier early; they must offer payment plans and there may be hardship schemes
questions.explanation: Suppliers have obligations to offer affordable arrangements, and early contact keeps options open.

questions.question: Bills in your name but for a previous home can mean:
options: Chasing debt later, so always take final meter readings and give a forwarding address when moving
questions.explanation: Close accounts properly with final readings to avoid debts following you.
